reminder: A set of vectors spans a [vector space](c:vector-space) when every vector is a [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of them.
definition: A subset $S$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a spanning set when every vector of $V$ is a [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of finitely many vectors of $S$. Equivalently, the smallest subspace of $V$ that contains $S$ is $V$ itself.
examples: The vectors $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ span $\mathbb{R}^2$.
The three vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ also span $\mathbb{R}^2$, although one of them is not needed.
Non-example: the vectors $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$ do not span $\mathbb{R}^3$, because $(0,0,1)$ is not a linear combination of them.

steps: Start with a spanning set $S$ of a vector space $V$.
Add the condition that $S$ is [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset).
A spanning set that is linearly independent is a [basis of a vector space](c:basis-of-a-vector-space).
links.why: It shows that a basis is a spanning set without any redundant vector.

reminder: For each [partition](c:integer-partition) $\lambda$ of $n$, the Specht module $S^\lambda$ is a [representation](c:group-representation) of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$.
definition: Let $\lambda$ be a [partition](c:integer-partition) of $n$, let $k$ be a [field](c:field), and let $M^\lambda$ be the $k$-[vector space](c:vector-space) with one basis vector for each tabloid of shape $\lambda$, where a tabloid is a filling of the [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) of $\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ taken up to the order of the entries in each row. For a filling $t$ with column group $C_t$, the polytabloid is $e_t=\sum_{\sigma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\sigma\{t\}$, where $\{t\}$ is the tabloid of $t$. The Specht module $S^\lambda$ is the subspace of $M^\lambda$ spanned by all $e_t$, and it is a module over the [group ring](c:group-ring) $k[S_n]$.
examples: For $\lambda=(n)$, the Specht module is the trivial representation of $S_n$, and its dimension is $1$.
For $\lambda=(1^n)$, the Specht module is the sign representation of $S_n$.
Over $\mathbb{C}$, the modules $S^\lambda$ for all partitions $\lambda$ of $n$ are exactly the irreducible representations of $S_n$.
Non-example: the permutation module $M^{(n-1,1)}$ is not a Specht module, because it has dimension $n$ while $S^{(n-1,1)}$ has dimension $n-1$.

steps: A module over the [group ring](c:group-ring) $k[S_n]$ is the same as a $k$-linear representation of $S_n$.
For every permutation $\sigma$ we have $\sigma e_t=e_{\sigma t}$, so the space $S^\lambda$ is stable under $S_n$.
So $S_n$ acts linearly on $S^\lambda$, and $S^\lambda$ is a [group representation](c:group-representation).
links.why: It lets a learner use all facts about group representations for each Specht module.

reminder: The special orthogonal group $SO(n)$ is the group of rotations of $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, orthogonal matrices of [determinant](c:determinant) $1$.
definition: The group $SO(n)$ is the set of real $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ with $A^{T}A=I$ and [determinant](c:determinant) equal to $1$, with matrix multiplication as the group law. It is the subgroup of the [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) of maps that keep orientation, and it acts on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ by rotations about the origin.
examples: $SO(2)$ is the group of plane rotations, with one rotation matrix for each angle $\theta$.
$SO(3)$ is the group of rotations of ordinary space, and each element is a rotation about an axis through the origin.
Non-example: the reflection $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ is orthogonal but has determinant $-1$, so it is not in $SO(2)$.

steps: Every element of $SO(n)$ is an orthogonal matrix.
The determinant of an orthogonal matrix is $1$ or $-1$, because $\det(A)^2=\det(A^{T}A)=1$.
So $SO(n)$ is the kernel of the determinant map from the [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) to $\{1,-1\}$.
It follows that $SO(n)$ has index $2$ in the orthogonal group, and the other coset holds the reflections.
links.why: It shows that $SO(n)$ is the orientation-preserving part of the orthogonal group.

steps: Take $n=2$ and write each element of $SO(2)$ as the rotation by an angle $\theta$.
Send this rotation to the complex number $e^{i\theta}$ of absolute value $1$.
This map is an isomorphism, because rotation by $\theta$ followed by rotation by $\varphi$ is rotation by $\theta+\varphi$.
So $SO(2)$ is the [circle group](c:circle-group).
links.why: It shows that the circle group is the first case of the rotation groups.

reminder: A specialization replaces a parameter in a [polynomial](c:polynomial) by a value of the base [field](c:field).
definition: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) and let $f(t,X)$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) in $X$ whose coefficients are [rational functions](c:rational-function) of $t$ over $K$. For a value $a\in K$ at which no coefficient has a pole, the specialization of $f$ at $t=a$ is the polynomial $f(a,X)\in K[X]$, obtained by replacing $t$ by $a$ in every coefficient.
examples: For $f(t,X)=X^2-t$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, the specialization at $t=4$ is $X^2-4$, which factors as $(X-2)(X+2)$.
The same $f$ specialized at $t=2$ gives $X^2-2$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Non-example: $f(t,X)=X-1/t$ has no specialization at $t=0$, because the coefficient $1/t$ has a pole there.

steps: Let $R\subseteq K(t)$ be the ring of rational functions that have no pole at $a$.
Evaluation at $t=a$ maps $R$ to $K$ and respects sums and products.
So evaluation is a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) from $R$ to $K$.
Apply it to every coefficient of $f$ to get the specialization $f(a,X)$.
links.why: It shows that a specialization respects sums and products of polynomials.

reminder: A spectral measure assigns to each measurable set an [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), and it is countably additive.
definition: Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) and $H$ a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). A spectral measure, also called a projection-valued measure, is a map $E$ that sends each $A\in\Sigma$ to an [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) $E(A)$ on $H$, with $E(X)=I$ and $E(\bigcup_n A_n)v=\sum_n E(A_n)v$ for all $v\in H$ and all disjoint sequences $(A_n)$ in $\Sigma$. It follows that $E(A\cap B)=E(A)E(B)$, and each unit vector $v$ gives a probability measure $A\mapsto\langle E(A)v,v\rangle$.
examples: For the diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ goes to the diagonal projection $E(A)$ onto the coordinates $i$ with $\lambda_i\in A$.
On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, the map that sends a Borel set $A$ to multiplication by the indicator function $1_A$ is a spectral measure.
Non-example: for the uniform probability measure $\mu$ on $[0,1]$, the map $A\mapsto\mu(A)I$ is not spectral, because $\mu([0,1/2])I=\tfrac12I$ is not a projection.

reminder: A spherical fibration is a [fibration](c:fibration) whose fibres are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to a [sphere](c:sphere).
definition: A spherical fibration is a [fibration](c:fibration) $p:E\to B$ such that every fibre $p^{-1}(b)$ is [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^{n-1}$ for some $n$. The fibres of a fibration over a connected base all have the same homotopy type, so $n$ does not depend on $b$.
examples: The unit sphere bundle of a real vector bundle of rank $n$ is a spherical fibration with fibre $S^{n-1}$.
The Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ has fibre $S^1$, so it is a spherical fibration.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ with $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$ is a fibration, but its fibre is the set of integers, which is not homotopy equivalent to a sphere.

steps: Let $p:E\to B$ be a [fibration](c:fibration) over a connected base.
Add the condition that each fibre has the homotopy type of a sphere.
Then $p$ is a spherical fibration.
links.why: It shows that a spherical fibration is a fibration with one extra condition on its fibres.

steps: Start with a [sphere fiber bundle](c:sphere-fiber-bundle) $E\to B$ with fibre $S^{n-1}$.
A fibre bundle is locally trivial, so it is a fibration in the sense of Serre.
Its fibres are spheres, so they are homotopy equivalent to $S^{n-1}$.
Hence $E\to B$ is a spherical fibration, but the converse fails, because a fibration need not be locally trivial.
links.why: It shows that spherical fibrations are the homotopy-invariant version of sphere bundles.

reminder: A spherical space form is the quotient of a round [sphere](c:round-sphere) by a group of isometries that acts freely.
definition: A spherical space form is the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) $S^n/G$ of the round [sphere](c:round-sphere) $S^n$, with $n\ge2$, by a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $G$ of its [isometry group](c:isometry-group) that acts [freely](c:free-action) and [properly discontinuously](c:properly-discontinuous-action). Such a quotient is a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of constant positive curvature, and $G$ must be finite.
examples: The real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^n=S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is a spherical space form, and the antipodal map is the only element of $G$ besides the identity.
Each lens space $L(p;q)=S^3/\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a spherical space form, where a generator acts by $(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/p}z,e^{2\pi iq/p}w)$ and $\gcd(p,q)=1$.
Non-example: the quotient of $S^2$ by the rotation through angle $\pi$ about an axis is not a spherical space form, because the two poles stay fixed and so the action is not free.

steps: Take $G=\{\pm1\}$ acting on $S^n$ by the antipodal map $x\mapsto-x$.
This map is an isometry and it has no fixed point, so the action is free.
The action is properly discontinuous, because $G$ is finite.
The quotient $S^n/G$ is the [real projective space](c:real-projective-space).
links.why: It shows that real projective spaces are the simplest spherical space forms.

steps: Give $S^n$ the round metric, which has constant positive curvature.
Since $G$ acts freely and properly discontinuously, the quotient map is a covering map.
Each element of $G$ is an isometry, so the round metric descends to $S^n/G$.
Hence $S^n/G$ is a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with constant positive curvature.
links.why: It shows that every spherical space form carries a canonical metric of constant positive curvature.

reminder: The spin group $Spin(n)$ is a connected double cover of the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group) $SO(n)$.
definition: The spin group $Spin(n)$ is the group of all products of an even number of unit vectors in the [Clifford algebra](c:clifford-algebra) of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Conjugation $v\mapsto gvg^{-1}$ by an element $g$ rotates the vectors, and it gives a surjective homomorphism $Spin(n)\to SO(n)$ with kernel $\{1,-1\}$. For $n\ge3$ the group $Spin(n)$ is simply connected, so it is the [universal covering space](c:universal-covering-space) of $SO(n)$ and a [double cover](c:double-cover) of it.
examples: $Spin(3)$ is the group of unit quaternions, which is isomorphic to the [special unitary group](c:special-unitary-group) $SU(2)$, and it double covers $SO(3)$.
$Spin(2)$ is a circle, and it covers the circle $SO(2)$ twice by $z\mapsto z^2$.
Non-example: $SO(3)$ is not $Spin(3)$, because $SO(3)$ is not simply connected, and its fundamental group is $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

steps: The invertible elements of the finite-dimensional algebra $Cl(\mathbb{R}^n)$ form a Lie group, and $Spin(n)$ is a closed subgroup of it.
A closed subgroup of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) is again a Lie group.
So $Spin(n)$ is a Lie group, and it has the same Lie algebra as $SO(n)$, because it covers $SO(n)$.
links.why: It shows that all facts about Lie groups apply to the spin group.

steps: Take $n=2$, so $SO(2)$ is the circle group of plane rotations.
Its connected double cover is again a circle, and the covering map is $z\mapsto z^2$.
This double cover is the group $Spin(2)$.
links.why: It gives a first concrete case of the double cover that defines the spin group.

reminder: A spinor bundle on a [spin manifold](c:spin-manifold) is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) associated to its spin structure by a [spin representation](c:spin-representation).
definition: Let $M$ be a [spin manifold](c:spin-manifold) of dimension $n$, let $P\to M$ be a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) with structure group $Spin(n)$ that lifts the frame bundle of the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle), and let $\rho$ be a [spin representation](c:spin-representation) of the [spin group](c:spin-group) on a vector space $\Delta$. The spinor bundle is the [associated bundle](c:associated-bundle) $S=P\times_{\rho}\Delta$, and its sections are the spinor fields on $M$.
examples: On a spin manifold of dimension $n$, the complex spinor bundle built from the complex spin representation has rank $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.
On flat $\mathbb{R}^3$, the spinor bundle is the trivial bundle $\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{C}^2$.
Non-example: the complex projective plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$ has no spin structure, so it has no spinor bundle.

steps: Let $P\to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle and let $\rho$ be a representation of $G$ on a vector space $V$.
The [associated bundle](c:associated-bundle) $P\times_\rho V$ is a vector bundle with fibre $V$.
Take $G=Spin(n)$, take $P$ to be the spin structure, and take $\rho$ to be a spin representation.
Then $P\times_\rho V$ is the spinor bundle.
links.why: It shows that a spinor bundle is an associated bundle built from the spin structure.

steps: The fibre of $S=P\times_\rho\Delta$ over each point of $M$ is a copy of the vector space $\Delta$.
Local trivializations of $P$ give local trivializations of $S$ with linear transition functions $\rho(g)$.
So $S$ is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) over $M$.
It adds that the transition functions come from $Spin(n)$, so tangent vectors act on $S$ by Clifford multiplication.
links.why: It shows what a spinor bundle adds to a vector bundle: a Clifford action of tangent vectors.

reminder: Two closed [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) of dimension $2n$ are stably diffeomorphic when they become [diffeomorphic](c:diffeomorph) after connected sums with copies of $S^n\times S^n$.
definition: Two closed connected [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and $N$ of dimension $2n$ are stably diffeomorphic when $M\#r(S^n\times S^n)$ and $N\#s(S^n\times S^n)$ are [diffeomorphic](c:diffeomorph) for some integers $r,s\ge0$. Here $\#$ is the connected sum, and $r(S^n\times S^n)$ is the connected sum of $r$ copies.
examples: Diffeomorphic manifolds are stably diffeomorphic: take $r=s=0$.
Every $M$ is stably diffeomorphic to $M\#(S^n\times S^n)$: take $r=1$ and $s=0$.
By a theorem of Wall, two closed simply connected smooth 4-manifolds with isomorphic intersection forms are stably diffeomorphic.
Non-example: $S^4$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2$ are not stably diffeomorphic, because their signatures are $0$ and $1$, and connected sums with $S^2\times S^2$ do not change the signature.

steps: Let $M$ and $N$ be closed smooth $2n$-manifolds that are [diffeomorphic](c:diffeomorph).
Take $r=s=0$ in the definition of stable diffeomorphism.
Then $M\#0(S^n\times S^n)=M$ and $N\#0(S^n\times S^n)=N$ are diffeomorphic by assumption.
The converse fails, because $M$ and $M\#(S^n\times S^n)$ have different Betti numbers.
links.why: It shows that stable diffeomorphism is a weaker relation than diffeomorphism.

reminder: A stable [∞-category](c:infinity-1-category) has a zero object and finite limits and colimits, and a square is a pullback exactly when it is a pushout.
definition: A stable ∞-category is an [∞-category](c:infinity-1-category) $C$ with a zero object, in which every diagram that is finite has a limit and a colimit, and in which a commutative square is a [pullback](c:pullback) if and only if it is a [pushout](c:pushout). Then suspension and loops are inverse equivalences, and the homotopy category of $C$ is a [triangulated category](c:triangulated-category).
examples: The ∞-category of spectra is stable.
The derived ∞-category of an abelian category, built from chain complexes up to quasi-isomorphism, is stable.
Non-example: the ∞-category of spaces is not stable, because it has no zero object: its terminal object is a point and its initial object is the empty space.

steps: Start with an [∞-category](c:infinity-1-category) $C$.
Add the conditions that $C$ has a [zero object](c:has-zero-object) and all [finite limits](c:finite-limit) and finite colimits.
Add the condition that the pullback squares of $C$ and the pushout squares of $C$ are the same.
Then $C$ is a stable ∞-category.
links.why: It shows that stability is a short list of conditions on an ordinary ∞-category.

reminder: For large frequency, the stationary phase approximation says that an oscillatory integral is dominated by the [critical points](c:critical-point) of its phase.
definition: Let $a$ be a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) with [compact support](c:compact-support) on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\phi$ be a real smooth function whose only critical point on the support of $a$ is a [nondegenerate critical point](c:nondegenerate-critical-point) $x_0$ with [Hessian](c:hessian) $H$. Then $\int a(x)e^{i\lambda\phi(x)}\,dx=\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\right)^{n/2}\frac{e^{i\pi\operatorname{sgn}(H)/4}}{\sqrt{|\det H|}}\,a(x_0)e^{i\lambda\phi(x_0)}\,(1+O(1/\lambda))$ as $\lambda\to\infty$. The full [asymptotic expansion](c:asymptotic-expansion) has further terms of higher order in $1/\lambda$.
examples: For $\int e^{i\lambda x^2}dx$ over $\mathbb{R}$, the phase $x^2$ has the critical point $0$ with $H=2$, and the integral equals exactly $\sqrt{\pi/\lambda}\,e^{i\pi/4}$.
For $J_0(\lambda)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i\lambda\cos\theta}d\theta$, the critical points $0$ and $\pi$ give $J_0(\lambda)\approx\sqrt{2/(\pi\lambda)}\cos(\lambda-\pi/4)$.
Non-example: for the phase $\phi(x)=x$ there is no critical point, and $\int a(x)e^{i\lambda x}dx$ decays faster than every power of $1/\lambda$, so there is no leading term of power size.

reminder: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) is stationary when shifting time does not change its joint distributions.
definition: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ with time set $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}$ is stationary when, for all times $t_1,\dots,t_k$ and every shift $h$, the vectors $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_k})$ and $(X_{t_1+h},\dots,X_{t_k+h})$ have the same joint [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution). A process with finite second moments is weakly stationary when its mean is constant and the covariance of $X_s$ and $X_t$ depends only on $t-s$.
examples: An [iid sequence](c:iid-random-variables) $(X_n)$ is stationary, because every shift gives the same product distribution.
A [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) that starts in its stationary distribution is a stationary process.
Non-example: the random walk $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$ with iid steps of mean $0$ and variance $1$ is not stationary, because $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=n$ changes with $n$.

steps: Let $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with common law $\mu$.
For times $n_1<\dots<n_k$, the vector $(X_{n_1},\dots,X_{n_k})$ has law $\mu^{\otimes k}$.
The vector at the shifted times $n_i+h$ also has law $\mu^{\otimes k}$.
So the sequence is stationary.
links.why: It shows that every iid sequence is stationary, and that stationary processes also allow dependence.

steps: Take a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ with time set $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}$.
Add the condition that all finite-dimensional joint laws are unchanged by a time shift.
Then the process is stationary.
links.why: It shows that stationarity is a symmetry condition on the laws of the process.

reminder: A stochastic process is a family of [random variables](c:random-variable) indexed by a linearly ordered set, which is usually time.
definition: A stochastic process is a family $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) on one probability space, with values in a common [measurable space](c:measurable-space), where the index set $T$ is a [totally ordered set](c:total-order) such as $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ or $[0,\infty)$, read as time. Equivalently, it is one random variable whose values are paths, that is, functions from $T$ to the value space.
examples: Coin tossing is a stochastic process with $T=\mathbb{N}$, where $X_n$ is the result of the $n$th toss.
[Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a stochastic process with $T=[0,\infty)$.
Non-example: two random variables on two unrelated probability spaces do not form a stochastic process, because they have no joint law.

steps: Start with a stochastic process $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ with values in a countable set.
Add the Markov condition: given $X_n$, the next value $X_{n+1}$ does not depend on $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$.
Then the process is a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain).
links.why: It shows that a Markov chain is a stochastic process with a memory condition.

steps: Start with a stochastic process $(X_n)$ adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_n)$, with $E|X_n|<\infty$.
Add the condition $E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n$ for every $n$.
Then $(X_n)$ is a [martingale](c:martingale).
links.why: It shows that a martingale is a stochastic process with a fair-game condition.

steps: Start with a stochastic process $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ with $B_0=0$.
Add the conditions that its increments are independent and that $B_t-B_s$ is normal with mean $0$ and variance $t-s$.
Add the condition that almost every path is continuous.
Then the process is [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion).
links.why: It shows that Brownian motion is the stochastic process with independent normal increments and continuous paths.

reminder: A term is strongly normalizing when every sequence of [reductions](c:beta-reduction) that starts at it ends after finitely many steps.
definition: In a [rewriting system](c:rewriting-system) with reduction relation $\to$, a term $t$ is strongly normalizing when there is no infinite sequence $t\to t_1\to t_2\to\cdots$. A system is strongly normalizing when all its terms are, and then every term reaches a [normal form](c:normal-form) however one chooses the reductions.
examples: Every term of the simply typed [lambda calculus](c:lambda-calculus) is strongly normalizing under [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction).
In the system on strings with the single rule $ba\to ab$, every string is strongly normalizing, because each step removes one inverted pair of letters.
Non-example: the term $\Omega=(\lambda x.xx)(\lambda x.xx)$ is not strongly normalizing, because $\Omega\to\Omega\to\cdots$ is an infinite reduction.

reminder: A subbasis of a topology is a family of sets whose finite intersections form a [basis of a topology](c:is-topological-basis).
definition: A family $\mathcal S$ of subsets of a set $X$ is a subbasis of a topology $\tau$ on $X$ when the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal S$, with $X$ as the empty intersection, form a [basis of a topology](c:is-topological-basis) for $\tau$. Equivalently, $\tau$ is the coarsest topology on $X$ that contains $\mathcal S$, so its [open sets](c:open-set) are exactly the unions of finite intersections of sets of $\mathcal S$.
examples: The open rays $(a,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,b)$ form a subbasis of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$.
The sets $\pi_i^{-1}(U)$ with $U$ open in $X_i$ form a subbasis of the [product topology](c:product-topology) on $\prod_i X_i$.
Non-example: the family $\{(0,2),(1,3)\}$ is not a subbasis of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$, because it generates a topology with only six open sets, and $(0,1)$ is not one of them.

steps: Let $\mathcal B$ be a basis of a topology $\tau$.
Finite intersections of members of $\mathcal B$ are open, so each is a union of members of $\mathcal B$.
Every member of $\mathcal B$ is already a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal B$, so every open set is a union of finite intersections.
So $\mathcal B$ is also a subbasis of $\tau$.
links.why: It shows that a subbasis is the weaker requirement: every basis is a subbasis.

reminder: A subdirect product is a subalgebra of a [direct product](c:direct-product) whose projection to each factor is [surjective](c:surjection).
definition: A subdirect product of a family of algebras $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, such as groups or rings, is a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) $B\le\prod_{i\in I}A_i$ such that each coordinate projection $\pi_i:B\to A_i$ is [surjective](c:surjection). Equivalently, an algebra $A$ is a subdirect product of the $A_i$ when there is an injective homomorphism $A\to\prod_iA_i$ with all coordinate maps surjective.
examples: The full direct product $\prod_iA_i$ is a subdirect product of the $A_i$, because each projection is onto.
The diagonal $\{(x,x):x\in G\}$ of $G\times G$ is a subdirect product of $G$ and $G$.

The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ embeds in $\prod_{n\ge1}\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ by $x\mapsto(x\bmod n)_n$ with all projections onto, so $\mathbb{Z}$ is a subdirect product of the rings $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

Non-example: the subgroup $\mathbb{Z}\times\{0\}$ of $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ is not a subdirect product of $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$, because its projection to the second factor is not surjective.

steps: Take algebras $A_i$ and form the [direct product](c:direct-product) $A=\prod_iA_i$.
Take $B=A$ as a subalgebra of itself.
Every coordinate projection $A\to A_i$ is surjective, because algebras are not empty.
So $A$ is a subdirect product of the $A_i$.
links.why: It shows that the direct product is the largest subdirect product.

steps: Let $B$ be a subdirect product of the algebras $A_i$.
By definition, $B$ is a [subalgebra](c:subalgebra) of the product $\prod_iA_i$.
It carries the extra condition that every projection $B\to A_i$ is surjective.
links.why: It shows that a subdirect product is a subalgebra of the product with one extra condition.

reminder: A submersion is a smooth map whose [differential](c:differential) is [surjective](c:surjection) at every point.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold). A [smooth map](c:smooth-function) $f:X\to Y$ is a submersion when, for every $x\in X$, the differential $df_x:T_xX\to T_{f(x)}Y$ between [tangent spaces](c:tangent-space) is a [surjective](c:surjection) linear map. Then every non-empty fibre $f^{-1}(y)$ is a smooth submanifold of dimension $\dim X-\dim Y$.
examples: The projection $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is a submersion.
The Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$ is a submersion, and its fibres are circles.
Non-example: the map $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x)=x^2$ is not a submersion, because $df_0=0$ is not surjective.

steps: Start with a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f:X\to Y$ between smooth manifolds.
Add the condition that $df_x$ is surjective for every $x\in X$.
Then $f$ is a submersion.
links.why: It shows that a submersion is a smooth map with one pointwise condition on its differential.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [local diffeomorphism](c:local-diffeomorphism).
Its differential $df_x$ is an isomorphism at every $x$, and an isomorphism is surjective.
So $f$ is a submersion.
Conversely, a submersion with $\dim X=\dim Y$ is a local diffeomorphism, by the inverse function theorem.
links.why: It shows that local diffeomorphisms are the submersions between manifolds of equal dimension.

reminder: The $i$th successive minimum is the smallest factor by which a [convex body](c:convex-body) must grow to contain $i$ independent lattice vectors.
definition: Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a [convex body](c:convex-body) that is symmetric about the origin, and let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of rank $n$. For $i=1,\dots,n$, the $i$th successive minimum $\lambda_i$ is the infimum of all $\lambda>0$ such that $\lambda K$ contains $i$ [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset) vectors of $\Lambda$, so $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_n$.
examples: For $K$ the closed unit ball and $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}^n$, all $\lambda_i$ equal $1$, because $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are independent lattice vectors of length $1$.
For $K=[-1,1]^2$ and $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}(1,0)+\mathbb{Z}(0,3)$, we get $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_2=3$.
Non-example: in the last case $\lambda_2$ is not $1$, although $K$ contains the two non-zero lattice vectors $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$, because these two vectors are linearly dependent.

reminder: A sum is the result of adding two or more [numbers](c:number), or other quantities, together.
definition: The sum of $a_1,\dots,a_n$ is the result $a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n$ of adding them in order, written $\sum_{k=1}^na_k$, and the empty sum is $0$. The same definition works in any [monoid](c:monoid) written additively, and the sum of an infinite [series](c:series) is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of its [partial sums](c:partial-sum).
examples: $1+2+3+4=10$, and in general $\sum_{k=1}^nk=n(n+1)/2$.
The series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty2^{-k}$ has sum $2$, because its partial sums $2-2^{-n}$ tend to $2$.
Non-example: the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty(-1)^k$ has no sum, because its partial sums alternate between $1$ and $0$ and have no limit.

steps: Take a sequence $(a_k)$ of numbers and a number $n$.
The [partial sum](c:partial-sum) $s_n$ is the sum $a_1+\dots+a_n$ of the first $n$ terms.
So each partial sum is a sum of the kind defined above, with a particular choice of terms.
The sum of the series is then the limit of these sums.
links.why: It shows that a partial sum is a plain sum of the first terms, and that infinite sums are built from finite ones.

reminder: A super-Cartan geometry is a [Cartan geometry](c:cartan-geometry) in which the manifold and the group are a [supermanifold](c:supermanifold) and a [supergroup](c:supergroup).
definition: Let $G$ be a [supergroup](c:supergroup) and $H\le G$ a closed sub-supergroup, with [Lie superalgebras](c:lie-superalgebra) $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$. A super-Cartan geometry modeled on $G/H$ is a [supermanifold](c:supermanifold) $X$ with an $H$-[principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $P\to X$ and a $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form $\omega$ on $P$, the Cartan connection, that is $H$-equivariant, restricts to the generating vector fields of the $H$-action, and gives an isomorphism $T_pP\to\mathfrak g$ at every point $p$.
examples: Every ordinary [Cartan geometry](c:cartan-geometry) is a super-Cartan geometry with no odd directions.

Take $G$ to be the super-Poincare group and $H$ the Lorentz group: a super-Cartan geometry modeled on $G/H$ is the geometric structure on which supergravity is built, before one adds torsion constraints.

Non-example: a supermanifold with an $H$-principal bundle and a principal connection with values in $\mathfrak h$ is not a super-Cartan geometry, because the form must take values in $\mathfrak g$ and identify $T_pP$ with $\mathfrak g$.

steps: Start with a [Cartan geometry](c:cartan-geometry) modeled on $G/H$, where $G$ is a Lie group and $X$ is a smooth manifold.
View $X$ as a supermanifold with no odd coordinates, and view $G$ and $H$ as supergroups with no odd directions.
The axioms of the Cartan connection $\omega$ stay the same, so $(P,\omega)$ is a super-Cartan geometry with no odd part.
Hence super-Cartan geometry contains Cartan geometry as its purely even case.
links.why: It shows that every result stated for super-Cartan geometries also covers ordinary Cartan geometries.

reminder: A supergroup is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of [supermanifolds](c:supermanifold), like a [Lie group](c:lie-group) with odd directions.
definition: A Lie supergroup is a [supermanifold](c:supermanifold) $G$ with smooth maps $m:G\times G\to G$, $e:*\to G$ and $i:G\to G$ that satisfy the axioms of a group as equalities of morphisms of supermanifolds, so $G$ is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of supermanifolds. Equivalently, for every supermanifold $S$ the set $G(S)$ of $S$-points is a group, naturally in $S$. The tangent space of $G$ at $e$ is a [Lie superalgebra](c:lie-superalgebra).
examples: Every [Lie group](c:lie-group) is a supergroup with no odd directions.
The odd line $\mathbb{R}^{0|1}$, with addition of the odd coordinate, is a supergroup whose underlying manifold is a point.
The general linear supergroup $GL(m|n)$ of invertible even supermatrices is a supergroup.
Non-example: no supermanifold with underlying manifold $S^2$ is a supergroup, because the underlying manifold of a supergroup is a Lie group and $S^2$ has no group structure.

steps: Let $G$ be a [Lie group](c:lie-group), viewed as a supermanifold with no odd coordinates.
Its multiplication, unit and inverse are smooth maps of supermanifolds, and the group axioms hold.
So $G$ is a supergroup whose odd part is zero.
Hence the supergroups with no odd directions are exactly the Lie groups.
links.why: It shows that supergroup theory contains Lie group theory as the case without odd directions.

steps: A group object in a category with finite products is an object $G$ with morphisms $m$, $e$ and $i$ that satisfy the group axioms.
Take the category of supermanifolds, which has finite products.
A [group object](c:group-object) in it is a supermanifold with smooth multiplication, unit and inverse.
That is a supergroup.
links.why: It shows that a supergroup is a group object, so general facts on group objects apply.

reminder: A function $f$ on a [lattice](c:lattice) is supermodular when $f(x\vee y)+f(x\wedge y)\ge f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x$ and $y$.
definition: Let $L$ be a [lattice](c:lattice) with join $\vee$ and [meet](c:meet) $\wedge$. A function $f:L\to\mathbb{R}$ with values in the [real numbers](c:real-number) is supermodular when $f(x\vee y)+f(x\wedge y)\ge f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y\in L$, and it is submodular when the inequality is reversed.
examples: A twice differentiable function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the componentwise order is supermodular if and only if $\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\ge0$ for all $i\ne j$, so $f(x)=x_1x_2$ is supermodular.
On the subsets of a finite set, ordered by inclusion, the function $f(A)=|A|^2$ is supermodular, because $f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)-f(A)-f(B)=2(|A|-|A\cap B|)(|B|-|A\cap B|)\ge0$.
Non-example: $f(x)=-x_1x_2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not supermodular, because $x=(1,0)$ and $y=(0,1)$ give $f(x\vee y)+f(x\wedge y)=-1$, which is less than $f(x)+f(y)=0$.

reminder: The support of a function is the [closure](c:closure) of the set of points where the function is not zero.
definition: Let $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. The support of $f$ is the [closure](c:closure) in $X$ of the set $\{x\in X:f(x)\ne0\}$, so it is the smallest closed set outside which $f$ is zero. For a distribution or a measure, the support is the complement of the largest [open set](c:open-set) on which it is zero.
examples: The function $f(x)=\max(0,1-|x|)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has support $[-1,1]$.
The function $f(x)=x$ has support $\mathbb{R}$, because the closure of $\{x:x\ne0\}$ is $\mathbb{R}$, although $f(0)=0$.
The Dirac measure $\delta_0$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has support $\{0\}$.
Non-example: for $f(x)=x$, the set $\{x:f(x)\ne0\}=\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is not the support, because a support is always closed.

reminder: A surface embedding draws a [graph](c:graph) on a [surface](c:surface) with edges as arcs that meet only at common ends.
definition: An embedding of a finite [graph](c:graph) $G$ in a [surface](c:surface) $\Sigma$ is a map that sends the vertices to distinct points and each edge to a simple arc between the images of its ends, such that two arcs meet only at a common end point. Equivalently, it is an [embedding of topological spaces](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces) from the topological realization of $G$ into $\Sigma$.
examples: Every [planar graph](c:planar-graph) has an embedding in the plane, and so in the sphere.
The complete graph $K_5$ embeds in the torus.
Non-example: the usual drawing of $K_5$ in the plane has crossing edges, so it is not an embedding, and in fact $K_5$ has no embedding in the plane.

steps: Take the surface $\Sigma$ to be the plane or the sphere.
A graph that has an embedding in this surface is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph).
So planar graphs are the graphs that have a surface embedding in the sphere.
links.why: It shows that planarity is the case of the sphere in the theory of surface embeddings.

steps: Form the topological realization $|G|$ of a finite graph $G$, with one point for each vertex and one arc for each edge.
A surface embedding of $G$ is an injective continuous map from $|G|$ to $\Sigma$.
Since $|G|$ is compact and $\Sigma$ is Hausdorff, this map is a homeomorphism onto its image.
So it is an [embedding of topological spaces](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces).
links.why: It shows that a surface embedding is a topological embedding of a one-dimensional space.

reminder: Surgery removes an embedded product of a sphere and a disk from a manifold and glues in a disk times a sphere.
definition: Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-[manifold](c:smooth-manifold) and let $\varphi:S^p\times D^{n-p}\to M$ be an embedding of a [sphere](c:sphere) times a closed disk. The result of surgery on $\varphi$ is $M'=\bigl(M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^{n-p})\bigr)\cup(D^{p+1}\times S^{n-p-1})$, glued along the common boundary $S^p\times S^{n-p-1}$ by $\varphi$. The trace of the surgery, obtained by attaching a $(p+1)$-handle to $M\times[0,1]$, is a [cobordism](c:cobordism) from $M$ to $M'$.
examples: Surgery on the thickened equator $S^1\times D^1\subset S^2$ removes an annulus and glues in $D^2\times S^0$, two disks, so it turns $S^2$ into $S^2\sqcup S^2$.
A Dehn surgery on a knot in $S^3$ is surgery with $n=3$ and $p=1$.
Non-example: removing a ball from $M$ and leaving the hole open is not surgery, because surgery glues in $D^{p+1}\times S^{n-p-1}$ along the boundary.

steps: Take $n=3$ and $p=1$, so the embedded piece is a solid torus $S^1\times D^2$ in a 3-manifold $M$.
Remove its interior and glue back a solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ along the boundary torus.
The gluing map decides which slope on the boundary torus bounds a disk in the new solid torus.
The result is [Dehn surgery](c:dehn-surgery) along the core knot with that slope.
links.why: It shows that Dehn surgery is the case of surgery on circles in 3-manifolds.

reminder: The suspension spectrum of a [pointed space](c:pointed-topological-space) $X$ has the $n$-fold [suspensions](c:suspension) of $X$ as its spaces.
definition: For a [pointed topological space](c:pointed-topological-space) $X$, the suspension spectrum $\Sigma^\infty X$ is the [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) whose $n$th space is the $n$-fold reduced [suspension](c:suspension) $\Sigma^nX$, with the identity maps $\Sigma(\Sigma^nX)\to\Sigma^{n+1}X$ as structure maps. Its homotopy groups are the stable homotopy groups of $X$, that is, $\pi_k(\Sigma^\infty X)=\operatorname{colim}_n\pi_{k+n}(\Sigma^nX)$.
examples: For $X=S^0$, the suspension spectrum is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum), whose $n$th space is $S^n$.
For $X$ a point, $\Sigma^\infty X$ is the zero spectrum, because all its spaces are points.
Non-example: an unpointed space $Y$ has no suspension spectrum until one chooses a base point, for example by forming $Y_+$.

steps: A [sequential spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) is a sequence of pointed spaces $E_n$ with maps $\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}$.
Put $E_n=\Sigma^nX$ for every $n\ge0$.
Take the structure maps $\Sigma\Sigma^nX\to\Sigma^{n+1}X$ to be the identity.
This gives a sequential spectrum, the suspension spectrum of $X$.
links.why: It shows that a suspension spectrum is a spectrum built from one pointed space by repeated suspension.

steps: Take the pointed space $X=S^0$, with two points and one of them as base point.
The $n$-fold reduced suspension of $S^0$ is the sphere $S^n$.
So $\Sigma^\infty S^0$ has $S^n$ as its $n$th space, with the identity structure maps.
That is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum).
links.why: It shows that the sphere spectrum is the suspension spectrum of the simplest pointed space.

reminder: The symmetric difference of two [sets](c:set) contains the elements that lie in exactly one of the two sets.
definition: The symmetric difference of sets $A$ and $B$ is $A\triangle B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$, the set of elements that belong to exactly one of $A$ and $B$. In terms of [exclusive disjunction](c:exclusive-disjunction), $A\triangle B=\{x:x\in A\text{ xor }x\in B\}$, and the indicator functions satisfy $1_{A\triangle B}=1_A+1_B\bmod2$.
examples: For every set $A$ we have $A\triangle A=\varnothing$ and $A\triangle\varnothing=A$, and the subsets of a set form a [Boolean ring](c:boolean-ring) with $\triangle$ as addition and $\cap$ as multiplication.
Non-example: the [union](c:union) $\{1,2,3\}\cup\{2,3,4\}=\{1,2,3,4\}$ is not the symmetric difference, because it keeps the common elements $2$ and $3$.

reminder: The $n$th symmetric product of a [space](c:topological-space) $X$ is the [quotient](c:quotient-space) of $X^n$ by permuting the coordinates.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and $n\ge1$, the $n$th symmetric product is $SP^n(X)=X^n/S_n$, the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) of the product $X\times\dots\times X$ by the [action](c:group-action) of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$ that permutes the factors. Its points are the unordered $n$-tuples $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ of points of $X$, where repeated points are allowed.
examples: $SP^n(\mathbb{C})\cong\mathbb{C}^n$, because an unordered $n$-tuple of complex numbers is the list of roots, with multiplicity, of a monic polynomial of degree $n$.
$SP^2(S^1)$ is the closed Mobius band.
Non-example: the ordinary product $X^2$ is not $SP^2(X)$, because $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$ are different points of $X^2$ but the same point of $SP^2(X)$.

steps: Let the symmetric group $S_n$ act on $X^n$ by permuting the coordinates.
Take the orbit space, which is the set of orbits with the quotient topology.
Each orbit is an unordered $n$-tuple, so the orbit space is $SP^n(X)$.
Thus $SP^n(X)$ is a [quotient space](c:quotient-space) of $X^n$ by a group action.
links.why: It shows that a symmetric product is an orbit space, so facts about quotients by group actions apply.

steps: Take $X=S^1$, the circle.
Then $SP^n(S^1)$ is the quotient of the torus $(S^1)^n$ by the permutation action.
This quotient is the [symmetric product of circles](c:symmetric-product-of-circles).
links.why: It shows that the symmetric product of circles is the first interesting case of the construction.

reminder: A symmetric set is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) whose $n$-simplices carry an [action](c:group-action) of $S_{n+1}$ that is compatible with faces and degeneracies.
definition: A symmetric set is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on the category of non-empty [finite sets](c:finite-set) and all maps between them. It assigns a set $X_n$ to $\{0,\dots,n\}$ and a map $X_m\to X_n$ to every map $\{0,\dots,n\}\to\{0,\dots,m\}$. Equivalently, it is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) with transposition maps $t^n_i:X_n\to X_n$ that generate an action of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_{n+1}$ on $X_n$ and obey compatibility relations with the faces and degeneracies.
examples: For any set $A$, the assignment $X_n=A^{n+1}$, with $S_{n+1}$ permuting the coordinates, is a symmetric set.
The nerve of a [groupoid](c:groupoid) is a symmetric set, with the transpositions built from inverse arrows.
Non-example: the simplicial set $\Delta^1$ with one edge from $0$ to $1$ has no transposition maps, because a transposition would have to send that edge to an edge from $1$ to $0$, and there is none.

steps: A symmetric set $X$ has a set $X_n$ for each $n$, and it has face and degeneracy maps.
Restrict the presheaf to the non-empty finite ordinals and the order-preserving maps.
The restriction is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set).
A symmetric set adds the action of $S_{n+1}$ on $X_n$ by the other maps.
links.why: It shows that a symmetric set is a simplicial set with extra symmetry.

reminder: A symplectic form is a nondegenerate alternating [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form), and on a manifold it is a closed 2-form that is nondegenerate at every point.
definition: A symplectic form on a real [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ that is alternating, so $\omega(v,v)=0$, and [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-form), so $\omega(v,w)=0$ for all $w$ only if $v=0$. On a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, a symplectic form is a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $2$ that is closed, so $d\omega=0$, and nondegenerate on each tangent space. Then $(M,\omega)$ is a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold).
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with coordinates $(x_1,\dots,x_n,y_1,\dots,y_n)$, the form $\omega=\sum_idx_i\wedge dy_i$ is symplectic.
The area form of an oriented surface is a symplectic form on that surface.
Non-example: no 2-form on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is symplectic, because a skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix has determinant $0$.

steps: Take a smooth manifold $M$ and a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $2$.
Add the condition that $\omega$ is closed, so that $d\omega=0$.
Add the condition that $\omega_p$ is nondegenerate on the tangent space at every point $p$.
Then $\omega$ is a symplectic form.
links.why: It shows that a symplectic form is a 2-form with two conditions: closed and nondegenerate.

steps: Take a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $\omega$ on a real vector space $V$.
Add the condition $\omega(v,v)=0$ for all $v$.
Add the condition that $\omega$ is nondegenerate.
At each point of a symplectic manifold, the form $\omega_p$ is such a form on the tangent space.
links.why: It shows that the pointwise algebra of a symplectic form is the linear algebra of alternating nondegenerate forms.

reminder: A map between [symplectic manifolds](c:symplectic-manifold) is symplectic when it pulls the form of the target back to the form of the source.
definition: Let $(M,\omega)$ and $(N,\sigma)$ be [symplectic manifolds](c:symplectic-manifold). A [smooth map](c:smooth-function) $f:M\to N$ is symplectic when the [pullback](c:pullback-of-a-differential-form) of $\sigma$ is $\omega$, that is, $f^*\sigma=\omega$. Then $df$ is injective at every point, because $\omega$ is nondegenerate, so a symplectic map between manifolds of equal dimension is a local diffeomorphism.
examples: Every translation $x\mapsto x+c$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is symplectic for the standard form.
The inclusion of the unit ball $B^{2n}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is a symplectic embedding, because both carry the standard form.
Non-example: the map $(x,y)\mapsto(2x,y)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\omega=dx\wedge dy$ is not symplectic, because it pulls $\omega$ back to $2\,dx\wedge dy$.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be a symplectic map that is also a diffeomorphism.
Then $f^{-1}$ is smooth, and $(f^{-1})^*\omega=(f^{-1})^*f^*\sigma=\sigma$, so $f^{-1}$ is symplectic too.
Such an $f$ is a [symplectomorphism](c:symplectomorphism).
links.why: It shows that a symplectomorphism is a symplectic map with a symplectic inverse.

steps: Start with a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f:M\to N$ between symplectic manifolds.
Add the condition that $f^*\sigma=\omega$.
Then $f$ is a symplectic map, and it is an immersion, because $\omega$ is nondegenerate.
links.why: It shows that a symplectic map is a smooth map that preserves the symplectic form.

reminder: Symplectic reduction restricts a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) to a level set of a [moment map](c:moment-map) and divides by the symmetry group.
definition: Let a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ act on a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) $(M,\omega)$ by a [Hamiltonian action](c:hamiltonian-action) with [moment map](c:moment-map) $\mu:M\to\mathfrak g^*$. Let $\mu_0$ be a regular value of $\mu$ whose stabilizer $G_{\mu_0}$ for the [coadjoint action](c:coadjoint-action) acts freely and properly on the level set $Z=\mu^{-1}(\mu_0)$. Then the reduced space $Z/G_{\mu_0}$ has a unique symplectic form whose pullback to $Z$ is the restriction of $\omega$.
examples: Reduce $\mathbb{C}^n$ by the circle action $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$ at the level $|z|^2=1$: the reduced space is $\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$ with a multiple of the Fubini-Study form.
If $G$ acts freely on a manifold $Q$, then reduction of $T^*Q$ at $\mu_0=0$ gives $T^*(Q/G)$.
Non-example: let $S^1$ rotate $\mathbb{C}$ with $\mu(z)=|z|^2/2$ and take $\mu_0=0$; the level set $\{0\}$ is a fixed point and $0$ is not a regular value, so the construction does not apply.

steps: Let $Z=\mu^{-1}(\mu_0)$ be the level set, with the restriction $\omega|_Z$ of the form.
The form $\omega|_Z$ is closed and has constant rank, so $(Z,\omega|_Z)$ is presymplectic.
At each point, the kernel of $\omega|_Z$ is the tangent space of the orbit of $G_{\mu_0}$.
Dividing $Z$ by these orbits is [presymplectic reduction](c:presymplectic-reduction), and it gives the symplectic reduction.
links.why: It shows that symplectic reduction is presymplectic reduction of a level set of the moment map.

reminder: A tail event of a sequence of [random variables](c:random-variable) does not depend on any finite set of its first terms.
definition: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be [random variables](c:random-variable) on a probability space. An event $A$ is a tail event when it lies in the [tail sigma-algebra](c:tail-sigma-algebra), which is the intersection over $n\ge1$ of the [sigma-algebras](c:sigma-algebra) $\sigma(X_n,X_{n+1},\dots)$. So for each $n$ the event $A$ is decided by $X_n,X_{n+1},\dots$ alone, and changing finitely many terms of the sequence does not change whether $A$ happens.
examples: The event that the sequence $(X_n)$ converges is a tail event.
The event that the series $\sum X_n$ converges is a tail event, and so is the event that $X_n\in B$ for infinitely many $n$.
Non-example: the event $\{X_1>0\}$ is not a tail event in general, because it depends on the first term.

steps: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be the probability space of the sequence.
Every tail event lies in $\sigma(X_n,X_{n+1},\dots)\subseteq\mathcal F$, so it is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set).
A tail event is a measurable set that also lies in the tail sigma-algebra.
links.why: It shows that a tail event is an ordinary event with one extra condition on how it depends on the sequence.

reminder: A [sphere](c:sphere) is tangent to a [plane](c:plane) or to another sphere when the two meet in exactly one point.
definition: A [sphere](c:sphere) is tangent to a [plane](c:plane) when they have exactly one common point, and this point is the foot of the perpendicular from the centre to the plane. Two spheres are tangent when they have exactly one common point, and then the two centres and that point lie on one line. A sphere is tangent to a surface at a point $P$ when it passes through $P$ and has the same [tangent plane](c:tangent-space) there.
examples: The unit sphere with centre $(0,0,1)$ is tangent to the plane $z=0$ at the origin.
Two spheres of radii $r<R$ whose centres are at distance $r+R$, or at distance $R-r$, are tangent.
The two Dandelin spheres of a plane section of a [cone](c:cone) each touch the cone and the plane, and they touch the plane at the foci of the [conic section](c:conic-section).
Non-example: the sphere of radius $1$ with centre $(0,0,1/2)$ meets the plane $z=0$ in a circle, not in one point, so it is not tangent to the plane.

reminder: A tangle is a compact 1-dimensional [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary) in a 3-cube whose boundary lies on two opposite faces.
definition: A tangle is a compact 1-dimensional [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary) $T$ embedded in the cube $[0,1]^3$ such that $T$ meets the [boundary](c:boundary) of the cube only in the boundary of $T$, and this boundary lies in the bottom face $[0,1]^2\times\{0\}$ and the top face $[0,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Its components are arcs and circles, and two tangles are the same when an [isotopy](c:isotopy) that fixes the boundary joins them.
examples: The $n$ vertical segments $\{p_i\}\times[0,1]$ with distinct points $p_i$ form a tangle, the trivial braid on $n$ strands.
A [knot](c:knot) or a [link](c:link) placed inside the cube is a tangle with empty boundary.
Non-example: a segment from the front face to the back face of the cube is not a tangle in this sense, because its end points are not on the bottom or top face.

steps: Let $L$ be a [link](c:link) in $\mathbb{R}^3$, a compact 1-manifold without boundary.
Move $L$ by an isotopy into the interior of the cube $[0,1]^3$.
Then $L$ meets the boundary of the cube in no point, and its own boundary is empty.
So $L$ is a tangle with no end points.
links.why: It shows that links are the tangles without end points.

steps: Let $K$ be a [knot](c:knot), a single embedded circle in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Move $K$ by an isotopy into the interior of the cube.
Then $K$ is a tangle with one component and empty boundary.
links.why: It shows that a knot is the simplest closed tangle, with one circle and no end points.

reminder: A $\tau$-function of the KP hierarchy is a function of infinitely many times that satisfies one bilinear identity.
definition: In the Sato theory of the KP hierarchy, write $\xi(t,z)=\sum_{k\ge1}t_kz^k$ and $[z^{-1}]=(z^{-1},z^{-2}/2,z^{-3}/3,\dots)$. A $\tau$-function is a function $\tau(t_1,t_2,\dots)$ that satisfies $\oint e^{\xi(t-t',z)}\,\tau(t-[z^{-1}])\,\tau(t'+[z^{-1}])\,dz=0$ for all $t$ and $t'$, where the integral is the [residue](c:residue) at $z=\infty$. Then $\psi(t,z)=e^{\xi(t,z)}\tau(t-[z^{-1}])/\tau(t)$ is a wave function that solves the KP hierarchy, and such $\tau$-functions correspond to points of the [Sato Grassmannian](c:sato-grassmannian).
examples: The constant function $\tau=1$ is a $\tau$-function, because $e^{\xi(t-t',z)}$ has no term in $z^{-1}$.
The function $\tau=1+e^{\xi(t,p)-\xi(t,q)}$ is a $\tau$-function for all numbers $p\ne q$, and it gives the one-soliton solution.

Non-example: the function $\tau(t)=t_2$ is not a $\tau$-function, because it violates the [Hirota equation](c:hirota-equation) $(D_1^4-4D_1D_3+3D_2^2)\tau\cdot\tau=0$: here $D_2^2\tau\cdot\tau=-2$ and the other terms are zero.

reminder: A telescoping [series](c:series) has terms of the form $b_n-b_{n+1}$, so its partial sums collapse to two terms.
definition: A [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ is telescoping when its terms are written as $a_n=b_n-b_{n+1}$ for an explicit sequence $(b_n)$, so that the middle terms of each [partial sum](c:partial-sum) cancel. Then $\sum_{n=1}^Na_n=b_1-b_{N+1}$, and the series converges if and only if $(b_n)$ has a [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence), and then its sum is $b_1-\lim b_n$.
examples: Since $\frac1{n(n+1)}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}$, the partial sums of $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n(n+1)}$ equal $1-\frac1{N+1}$, and the sum is $1$.
The reciprocals of the triangular numbers $n(n+1)/2$ give $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac2{n(n+1)}=2$ by the same collapse.
A telescoping series can diverge: $\ln(1+1/n)=\ln(n+1)-\ln n$, so the partial sums equal $\ln(N+1)$, which is unbounded.
Non-example: for $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^2$ no explicit $(b_n)$ is known, and every choice has the form $b_n=c-\sum_{k<n}1/k^2$, which contains the partial sums, so nothing cancels.

steps: Start with a [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ of real numbers.
Add the condition that $a_n=b_n-b_{n+1}$ for an explicit sequence $(b_n)$.
Then the partial sums collapse to $b_1-b_{N+1}$, and the series is a telescoping series.
links.why: It shows that a telescoping series is a series whose terms are differences of a simpler sequence.

reminder: The $n$th tensor power of an [object](c:object) $V$ is the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) of $n$ copies of $V$, and the $0$th power is the [unit object](c:unit-object).
definition: In a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) with tensor product $\otimes$ and [unit object](c:unit-object) $I$, the $n$th tensor power of an [object](c:object) $V$, for a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$, is given by $V^{\otimes0}=I$ and $V^{\otimes(n+1)}=V^{\otimes n}\otimes V$. Different bracketings of $V\otimes\dots\otimes V$ are isomorphic by the associator, so the bracketing does not matter up to canonical isomorphism.
examples: For a vector space $V$ with the usual tensor product, $V^{\otimes2}=V\otimes V$ has dimension $(\dim V)^2$, and $V^{\otimes0}$ is the ground field.
In the category of sets with the cartesian product, the $n$th tensor power of a set $S$ is the cartesian power $S^n$.
In the category of abelian groups, $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\otimes n}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ for every $n\ge1$.
Non-example: the direct sum $V\oplus V$ is not the tensor power $V^{\otimes2}$, because for $\dim V=3$ it has dimension $6$ while $V\otimes V$ has dimension $9$.

steps: Take a category $C$ with finite products, and use the cartesian product as the tensor product.
The unit object is then the terminal object $1$.
By induction, $V^{\otimes n}$ is the product $V\times\dots\times V$ with $n$ factors, up to canonical isomorphism.
So the tensor power is the [cartesian power](c:cartesian-power) $V^n$.
links.why: It shows that cartesian powers are the tensor powers of a cartesian monoidal category.

reminder: The term model of a [dependent type theory](c:dependent-type-theory) has the types and terms of the theory itself as its types and terms.
definition: Let $T$ be a [dependent type theory](c:dependent-type-theory). Its term model is the [model](c:model) of $T$ whose types and terms are those that the rules of [natural deduction](c:natural-deduction) of $T$ build, taken up to the equality that $T$ proves, with each type and term interpreted as itself. It is the [initial](c:initial-object) model of $T$, and its category of contexts is the [syntactic category](c:syntactic-category) of $T$.
examples: For the simply typed lambda calculus, the term model has the types as objects and the terms up to $\beta\eta$-equality as maps, and it is a cartesian closed category.
For the equational theory of groups, the terms in variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ modulo the group axioms form the free group on $n$ generators.
Non-example: the model in sets that interprets a base type $b$ by $\mathbb{N}$ is not the term model, because it has elements of $b$ while the theory has no closed term of type $b$.

steps: Interpret each type of $T$ as itself and each term of $T$ as itself, modulo equality.
Every rule of $T$ holds in this interpretation, because the types and terms were built with the rules of $T$.
So the interpretation is a [model](c:model) of $T$.
It is the initial model, because interpreting a term in another model gives the unique structure-preserving map.
links.why: It shows that the term model is a model, and the one that maps uniquely to every other model.

reminder: A tetrahedron is a [polyhedron](c:polyhedron) with four triangular faces, six edges and four vertices.
definition: A tetrahedron is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of four points in space that do not lie in one [plane](c:plane), and it has four triangular faces, six edges and four vertices. It is regular when all its faces are equilateral triangles of the same size, and then it is the Platonic solid with four faces.
examples: The points $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are the vertices of a tetrahedron, which is a corner of a cube.
The regular tetrahedron with vertices $(1,1,1)$, $(1,-1,-1)$, $(-1,1,-1)$ and $(-1,-1,1)$ has all six edges of length $2\sqrt2$.
Non-example: four points in one plane have a flat convex hull, so they do not form a tetrahedron.

steps: A [simplex](c:simplex) of dimension $n$ is the convex hull of $n+1$ points that are affinely independent.
Take $n=3$, so the points are four points that do not lie in one plane.
Their convex hull is a tetrahedron.
links.why: It shows that a tetrahedron is the 3-dimensional simplex.

reminder: The theta divisor of a principally polarized [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) is the divisor of zeros of the theta function, and it defines the polarization.
definition: Let $A=\mathbb{C}^g/(\mathbb{Z}^g+\tau\mathbb{Z}^g)$ be the [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) of a symmetric complex $g\times g$ matrix $\tau$ with positive definite imaginary part. The zero set in $\mathbb{C}^g$ of the [Riemann theta function](c:riemann-theta-function) $\theta(z,\tau)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^g}\exp(\pi i\,m^T\tau m+2\pi i\,m^Tz)$ is stable under the lattice, so it defines a [divisor](c:divisor) $\Theta$ on $A$, the theta divisor, which gives the principal [polarization](c:polarization) of $A$. For the [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety) of a smooth [curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g$, $\Theta$ is, up to translation, the set of sums of $g-1$ points of the curve.
examples: For $g=1$, the abelian variety $A$ is an elliptic curve and $\Theta$ is a single point.
For the Jacobian of a curve $C$ of genus $2$, $\Theta$ is a copy of $C$ inside the Jacobian.
Non-example: for $g\ge2$ a point of $A$ is not a theta divisor, because $\Theta$ has dimension $g-1\ge1$.

steps: The theta function is a section of a line bundle $L$ on $A$ that defines the principal polarization.
The zero set of a non-zero section of a line bundle is an effective [divisor](c:divisor).
The theta divisor is this divisor, and its class represents the polarization.
links.why: It shows that the theta divisor is a particular effective divisor, the zero locus of the theta function.

reminder: A thick subcategory is a full [triangulated subcategory](c:triangulated-subcategory) that is closed under [direct summands](c:direct-sum).
definition: A non-empty full [triangulated subcategory](c:triangulated-subcategory) $\mathcal T'$ of a [triangulated category](c:triangulated-category) $\mathcal T$ is thick when it is closed under direct summands: whenever $M\oplus N$ is isomorphic to an object of $\mathcal T'$, both $M$ and $N$ lie in $\mathcal T'$.
examples: In the derived category $D(R)$ of a ring $R$, the perfect complexes form a thick subcategory.
In $D(\mathbb{Z})$, the complexes whose cohomology groups vanish outside finitely many degrees form a thick subcategory.

Non-example: in the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $k$, the complexes whose total cohomology has even dimension form a triangulated subcategory that is not thick, because $k\oplus k$ lies in it but the summand $k$ does not.

steps: Start with a full [triangulated subcategory](c:triangulated-subcategory) $\mathcal T'$ of $\mathcal T$.
Add the condition that $M\oplus N\in\mathcal T'$ implies $M\in\mathcal T'$ and $N\in\mathcal T'$.
Then $\mathcal T'$ is thick.
links.why: It shows that thickness is one closure condition on a triangulated subcategory.

steps: Let $M$ be a direct summand of an object $X$ of a [localizing subcategory](c:localizing-subcategory) $\mathcal L$, with idempotent $e:X\to X$.
Then $M$ is the homotopy colimit of $X\xrightarrow{e}X\xrightarrow{e}\cdots$, which is a cone of a map between countable coproducts of copies of $X$.
A localizing subcategory contains such coproducts and cones, so $M$ lies in $\mathcal L$.
Hence every localizing subcategory is thick.
links.why: It shows that thickness is the weaker condition: every localizing subcategory is thick.

reminder: The third moment of a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $X^3$.
definition: For a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with $E|X|^3<\infty$, the third moment is $E[X^3]$, and the third central moment is $E[(X-\mu)^3]$ with $\mu=E[X]$. The absolute version $E|X-\mu|^3$ is the quantity that appears in the Berry-Esseen bound for the central limit theorem.
examples: If $X$ takes the values $1$ and $-1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each, then $E[X^3]=0$ and $E|X|^3=1$.
If $X$ is exponential with rate $1$, then $E[X^3]=3!=6$.
Non-example: a Cauchy random variable has no third moment, because $E|X|^3=\infty$.

steps: The $k$th [moment](c:moment) of a random variable $X$ is $E[X^k]$, whenever this expected value exists.
Fix the order $k=3$.
Then $E[X^3]$ is the third moment of $X$, and the central version replaces $X$ by $X-E[X]$.
links.why: It shows that the third moment is the case $k=3$ of the general moment.

reminder: The Thom space of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) is its disk bundle with the boundary [sphere bundle](c:sphere-bundle) collapsed to a point.
definition: Let $V\to X$ be a real [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) with an [orthogonal structure](c:orthogonal-structure), and let $D(V)$ and $S(V)$ be its bundles of unit disks and unit spheres. The Thom space is the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) $\mathrm{Th}(V)=D(V)/S(V)$, a pointed space whose base point is the collapsed sphere bundle. For compact $X$, it is the one-point compactification of the total space of $V$.
examples: Over a point, $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ and the Thom space is $D^n/S^{n-1}=S^n$.
For the trivial bundle $X\times\mathbb{R}^n$, the Thom space is the $n$-fold suspension of $X$ with a disjoint base point added.
For the tautological line bundle over $\mathbb{RP}^n$, the Thom space is $\mathbb{RP}^{n+1}$.
Non-example: the disk bundle $D(V)$ is not the Thom space, because its boundary sphere bundle is not collapsed, and $D(V)$ is homotopy equivalent to the base $X$.

reminder: A Thurston geometry is a simply connected [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) with a maximal transitive isometry group and at least one compact quotient manifold.
definition: A Thurston geometry is a pair $(X,G)$ where $X$ is a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-manifold) [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) and $G$ is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) that acts transitively on $X$ with compact point stabilizers. The pair must also satisfy two conditions: $G$ is maximal among such groups, and some discrete subgroup $\Gamma\le G$ acts freely on $X$ with $X/\Gamma$ compact. In dimension $3$ there are exactly eight such geometries: $S^3$, $\mathbb{E}^3$, $\mathbb{H}^3$, $S^2\times\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{H}^2\times\mathbb{R}$, $\widetilde{SL_2(\mathbb{R})}$, Nil and Sol.
examples: Hyperbolic 3-space $\mathbb{H}^3$ with its full isometry group is a Thurston geometry, and its compact quotients are the closed [hyperbolic 3-manifolds](c:hyperbolic-3-manifold).
The product $S^2\times\mathbb{R}$ with its full isometry group is a Thurston geometry, and $S^2\times S^1$ is a compact quotient.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^3$ with only the translation group acts transitively with trivial stabilizers, but the group is not maximal, because the full Euclidean group is larger.

steps: A [Klein geometry](c:klein-geometry) is a space $X=G/H$ where a Lie group $G$ acts transitively and $H$ is the stabilizer of a point.
A Thurston geometry is such a space where the stabilizer $H$ is compact.
It adds that $X$ is simply connected.
It adds that $G$ is maximal and that some discrete subgroup of $G$ gives a compact quotient.
links.why: It shows that a Thurston geometry is a Klein geometry with four extra conditions.

reminder: A topological monoid is a [monoid](c:monoid) with a topology for which the multiplication is continuous.
definition: A topological monoid is a [monoid](c:monoid) $(M,\cdot,1)$ together with a [topology](c:topological-space) on $M$ such that the multiplication $M\times M\to M$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) for the [product topology](c:product-topology) on $M\times M$. The unit $1$ is just an element of $M$, so it needs no further condition.
examples: The real numbers $(\mathbb{R},\cdot,1)$ under multiplication, with the usual topology.
The $n\times n$ real matrices under multiplication, with the topology of $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$.
Every monoid with the discrete topology, such as the natural numbers under addition.

Non-example: the integers under addition with the cofinite topology are not a topological monoid, because the preimage of the closed set $\{0\}$ is the set $\{(x,y):x+y=0\}$, which is not closed in the product topology.

steps: Start with a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$.
Add a topology on the set $M$.
Require that the multiplication $M\times M\to M$ is continuous.
Then $M$ is a topological monoid.
links.why: It shows that a topological monoid is a monoid with a compatible topology.

steps: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group).
Forget the inverse map of $G$, and keep the multiplication and the unit.
The multiplication is still continuous, so the result is a topological monoid.
A topological monoid is a topological group exactly when every element has an inverse and inversion is continuous.
links.why: It shows that a topological group is a topological monoid with continuous inverses.

reminder: A torsion point of an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) is a point $P$ with $nP=O$ for some positive integer $n$.
definition: Let $E$ be an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over a field $K$, with its [abelian group](c:abelian-group) law and identity point $O$. A point $P\in E(\overline K)$ is a torsion point when $nP=O$ for some integer $n\ge1$, and the least such $n$ is the [order](c:order-of-an-element) of $P$. The torsion points form a subgroup, and for $n$ prime to the characteristic of $K$ the points with $nP=O$ form a group isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$.
examples: The identity $O$ is a torsion point of order $1$.
On the curve $y^2=x^3-x$, the point $(0,0)$ has order $2$, because a point with $y=0$ is its own negative.
On the curve $y^2=x^3+1$, the point $(2,3)$ has order $6$.
Non-example: on the curve $y^2=x^3-2$, the point $(3,5)$ has infinite order, because by the Nagell-Lutz theorem a torsion point has $y=0$ or $y^2$ dividing $108$, and $25$ does not divide $108$.

reminder: For a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of finite index in $G$, the transfer is a [homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) from $G$ to the [abelianization](c:abelianization) of $H$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of finite index $n$ in a [group](c:group) $G$, and let $t_1,\dots,t_n$ be representatives of the right cosets $Ht_i$. For $g\in G$, write $t_ig=h_it_{\sigma(i)}$ with $h_i\in H$ and $\sigma$ a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The transfer is the map $V:G\to H/[H,H]$ with $V(g)=\prod_{i=1}^nh_i\,[H,H]$, and it is a group [homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) that does not depend on the choice of representatives.
examples: If $H=G$, then $n=1$ and the transfer is the quotient map $G\to G/[G,G]$.
If $G$ is abelian, then $V(g)=g^n$ for every $g\in G$.
Non-example: the product $\prod_ih_i$ taken in $H$ itself, without passing to $H/[H,H]$, is not well defined, because it depends on the order of the factors and on the representatives.

reminder: The transfer map of a finite [covering space](c:covering-space) $E\to B$ sends each simplex of $B$ to the sum of its lifts in $E$.
definition: Let $p:E\to B$ be an $n$-sheeted [covering space](c:covering-space). The transfer is the stable map $t:\Sigma^\infty B_+\to\Sigma^\infty E_+$ of [suspension spectra](c:suspension-spectrum) that sends, on homology, each singular simplex of $B$ to the sum of its $n$ lifts to $E$, so that $p_*\circ t_*$ is multiplication by $n$. For the double cover $S^\infty\to\mathbb{RP}^\infty$, composing the transfer with the collapse of $S^\infty$ to a point gives the map to the sphere spectrum that appears in the Kahn-Priddy theorem.
examples: For the trivial $n$-sheeted cover $B\times\{1,\dots,n\}\to B$, the transfer sends a class $x$ to $(x,\dots,x)$, with one copy in each sheet.
For the double cover $S^1\to S^1$ with $z\mapsto z^2$, the transfer sends the generator of $H_1$ of the base to the generator of $H_1$ of the cover, and $p_*$ doubles, so $p_*t_*=2$.
Non-example: the cover $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ has infinitely many sheets, so it has no such transfer, because the sum of the lifts of a point is infinite.
